title: A hymn in Sri Rag
hook: the four watches of the night picture a life from birth to old age (Sri Rag M1, ang 74)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sri Rag, and your line was the first raga. Did you do one thing at its slow pace? Today, one of its hymns, heard as a song. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

Vanjaariaa mitraa. O merchant friend. Those words run through a hymn of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, on ang seventy-four: they come in the first line of every stanza and again inside it, so a singer keeps coming back to them. Earlier on the path you read this hymn closely, the four watches of the night laid over a single life. Today the same hymn, but heard the way it was written to be heard: sung, slowly, in the grave evening raga you met yesterday. Today: a hymn in Sri Rag.
screen: `O MERCHANT FRIEND.` → `THE FOUR WATCHES, AGAIN.` → `THIS TIME, SUNG.`

segments.voice: On the page, the hymn is a map. In the first watch of the night, it says, by command a life is placed in the womb. In the second, the child is carried and adored. In the third, the mind turns to wealth and youth. In the fourth, the reaper comes to the field. Each stanza closes with Guru Nanak's name and a word to the mortal in that watch. Now hear it in Sri Rag. The raga is slow and grave, and its mood holds from stanza to stanza. The tune holds steady while the life inside it moves: womb, childhood, the busy middle, the last cold stretch. A whole night goes by in a few minutes of singing, and the music never hurries. That steadiness does something the page can't. It makes the listener sit through each watch at the same pace, the bright ones and the hard ones alike. And then, in every stanza, the call comes back. Vanjaariaa mitraa. Merchant friend. A trader is someone sent out with capital, expected to come back with something to show. A friend is someone who tells you the truth while there's still time to act on it. Sung again and again, the call stops being a label and becomes a voice at the door, knocking in each watch. So the question the hymn leaves isn't only which watch a person is in. It's quieter and more present than that. Right now, in this hour, which watch is it? That's today's line: which watch now. Tomorrow the music changes, to a raga from the Punjab's own soil.
screen: `FOUR WATCHES, ONE LIFE.` · `THE TUNE HOLDS STEADY AS LIFE MOVES.` · `THE CALL RETURNS IN EVERY STANZA.` · then, large: `WHICH WATCH NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen, and think of your watch. If you can find a recording of this hymn, the pehre of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, play it now and let the singing go on while you sit. If not, say the call softly once, vanjaariaa mitraa, and then sit in the quiet it leaves. Don't add up your whole life. Just ask about this hour: is it a beginning, a being-carried, a building, or a settling of accounts? Let the answer be small and honest. Then let the steady sound, or the steady breath, carry you through the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can answer the friend's call with one Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Sri Rag. Guru Nanak's four watches of the night, sung in a slow, grave raga that holds steady while a life moves through it, with the merchant friend called in every stanza. Today's word.
screen: `A HYMN IN SRI RAG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: which watch now. Three times today, at morning, midday and evening, stop for one breath and ask it of the hour you're in. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's pehre are sung in Sri Rag in kirtan, and Sikhs also read them in the Guru Granth Sahib as a reflection on the stages of a life.

fork.setup: a friend on the road at night calls you 'merchant'. why would the hymn picture a person as a trader?
options: because it's about trade routes in Punjab.
because a life is like capital, sent out to come back with something.
because the listeners were all merchants.
fork.reveal: a trader is sent out with capital and expected to return with something to show; the hymn asks what a life is being traded for, watch by watch.

original.note: Gurmukhi: O merchant friend, the call that returns in every stanza of Guru Nanak's pehre in Sri Rag.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem about the night.
what it means: a life in four watches, sung in a steady evening raga, with a friend calling at every stanza.

what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's pehre in Sri Rag (Ang 74) carry the address vanjaariaa mitraa in the first line of every stanza and again within it, and close each stanza with his name, so the form itself, sung in Sri Rag, turns the call into a refrain across the four watches.

sources.ref: Sri Rag Pehre M1, Ang 74 (pahilai paharai rain kai vanjaariaa mitraa…)

notes: Day 650 (y2) taught this pehre stanza by stanza; this day deliberately turns to the hymn as sung in Sri Rag (steady tune, returning address) to avoid repeating that lesson.
Confirm that each stanza of this pehre (Ang 74) opens with 'vanjaariaa mitraa' and closes with 'kahu naanak'; the script says so.
Summary of the four watches follows day 650's paraphrase; confirm.
'The tune doesn't change from stanza to stanza' describes strophic singing in one raga; a ragi may vary the melody, so a Keeper may want to soften it.
Original ਵਣਜਾਰਿਆ ਮਿਤ੍ਰਾ: confirm spelling (the Granth's spelling with ਮਿਤ੍ਰਾ) and pronunciation.

Editor: the address vanjaariaa mitraa does not open each stanza (it follows 'in the first watch of the night' and recurs inside each stanza); fixed hook, teach, word, games; cut the wrong 'sung four times'; fourth watch now 'the reaper comes to the field' (dropped unchecked 'accounts are read'); 'tune doesn't change' softened to 'its mood holds'.
